rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the fronting of “from them” to imply that people eat exclusively from livestock, since this is their principal livelihood and other foods are incidental; Abū Ḥayyān rejects fronting as a general marker of restriction.
rows.anchor: تقدم الظرف في قوله: ومنها تأكلون مؤذن، بالاختصاص وقد يؤكل من غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “from them” is partitive, as in saying one ate some of a loaf.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن من للتبعيض كقولك: إذا أكلت من الرغيف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He also explains people’s provisions as coming from livestock because cattle plow, while camels are hired out and their young, milk, and hides sold; on this reading min is figurative or causal.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن طعمتكم منها لأنكم تحرثون بالبقر، والحب والثمار التي تأكلونها منها

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī gives jamīl as the masculine, jamīlah and jamlāʾ as feminine forms, and derives jamāl from jamula.
rows.anchor: الجمال مصدر جمل بضم الميم، والرجل جميل، والمرأة جميلة وجملاء عن الكسائي

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: A cited poem uses jamlāʾ of a woman whose beauty surpasses everyone else’s.
rows.anchor: فهي جملاء كبدر طالع ... بزت الخلق جميعا بالجمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jamāl can mean beautification, as though it were a verbal noun with its augmentative letters omitted.
rows.anchor: ويطلق الجمال ويراد به التجمل، كأنه مصدر على إسقاط الزوائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beauty can be visual harmony perceived by sight, a quality of character such as knowledge, chastity, and forbearance, or deeds that benefit people and avert harm.
rows.anchor: والجمال يكون في الصورة بحسن التركيب يدركه البصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The beauty of livestock here is their social grandeur: possession signals worldly prosperity and brings owners esteem, alongside necessary practical benefits.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أنه لنا فيها جمال وعظمة عند الناس باقتنائها ودلالتها على سعادة الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Livestock adornment is itself a divine favor because herders seek it as a source of pride, and Arabs boast of their herds.
rows.anchor: فمن الله تعالى بالتجمل بها، كما من بالانتفاع الضروري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem contrasts a wealthy herd of camels with people whose sheep are followed by a leopard, illustrating pride in livestock.
rows.anchor: لعمري لقوم قد نرى أمس فيهم ... مرابط للإمهاز والعكر الدثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ʿakrah is a herd of sixty to seventy camels, and dathr means plentiful.
rows.anchor: والعكرة من الإبل ما بين الستين إلى السبعين، والجمع عكر. والدثر الكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Returning livestock from pasture is called irāḥah; taking them out in the morning is sarḥ, especially during spring growth after rain, when people migrate in search of grazing.
rows.anchor: ويقال: أراح الماشية ردها بالعشي من المرعى، وسرحها يسرحها سرحا وسروحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The returning herd looks most beautiful when full-bellied with full udders; at both outings its sounds delight the household and raise the owners’ standing.
rows.anchor: وقدم الإراحة على السرح لأن الجمال فيها أظهر إذا أقبلت ملأى البطون، حافلة الضروع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He supports the social value of livestock by linking adornment of worldly life and people’s love of desires with the mention of livestock and crops.
rows.anchor: المال والبنون زينة الحياة الدنيا وقوله تعالى: زين للناس حب الشهوات

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrimah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Jaḥdarī read ḥīnan in both clauses with nunation, breaking the genitive construction; the two clauses are adjectives with a deleted resumptive pronoun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة والضحاك والجحدري: حينا فيهما بالتنوين، وفك الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, the governing element of ḥīnan may be the subject, understood as “adornment,” or the predicate with its sense of existence.
rows.anchor: ويكون العامل في حينا على هذا، إما المبتدأ لأنه في معنى التجمل، وإما خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thiqal is given as the singular of athqāl; another interpretation takes athqāl as bodies, namely human bodies in the earth’s emergence at 99:2.
rows.anchor: الأمتعة: واحدها ثقل. وقيل: الأجسام لقوله تعالى: وأخرجت الأرض أثقالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destination is generally any distant land travelers intend to reach; named destinations are examples, since the favor of carrying loads applies beyond them.
rows.anchor: وينبغي حمل هذه الأقوال على التمثيل لا على المراد، إذ المنة لا تختص بالحمل إليها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas identify the destination as Mecca; other reports name Medina or Egypt.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد به معين وهو مكة، قاله: ابن عباس، وعكرمة، والربيع بن أنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about not reaching the destination may modify “land,” with an implied “by them,” stressing the distance and the hardship even with animals carrying the loads.
rows.anchor: ولم تكونوا بالغيه صفة للبلد، ويحتمل أن يكون التقدير بها، وذلك تنبيه على بعد البلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the sense is that without the animals people could not carry their loads on their backs and reach it without hardship.
rows.anchor: أو يكون التقدير: لم تكونوا بالغيه بأنفسكم دونها إلا بالمشقة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce shiq with kasrah; Mujāhid, al-Aʿraj, Abū Jaʿfar, ʿUmar ibn Maymūn, and Ibn Arqam read it with fatḥah, also reported from Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr; both forms mean hardship.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بشق بكسر الشين. وقرأ مجاهد، والأعرج، وأبو جعفر، وعمر بن ميمون، وابن أرقم: بفتحها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One lexical distinction makes shiq with fatḥah the verbal noun and shiq with kasrah the noun for hardship.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الشق بالفتح المصدر، وبالكسر الاسم، ويعني به: المشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem supplies evidence for shiq with kasrah meaning hardship.
rows.anchor: أذي إبل يسعى ويحسبها له ... أخي نصب من شقها ودؤوب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ takes shiq as half: the journey would exhaust half their lives, a figurative description of extreme toil; shiq also means a side or half, as in a half-sheep.
rows.anchor: وشق الشيء نصفه، وعلى هذا حمله الفراء هنا أي: يذهبان نصف الأنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning divine gentleness and mercy suits this favor because God facilitates these benefits and subjugates livestock.
rows.anchor: وناسب الامتنان بهذه النعمة من حملها الأثقال الختم بصفة الرأفة والرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After necessary livestock benefits, the passage turns to animal benefits that are useful but not essential.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى مننه بالأنعام ومنافعها الضرورية، ذكر الامتنان بمنافع الحيوان التي ليست بضرورية

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers put horses and the coordinated items in the accusative; Ibn Abī ʿAblah reads them in the nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: والخيل وما عطف عليه بالنصب عطفا على والأنعام. وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riding is named because it is the greatest benefit, but this does not imply that riding horses is forbidden, contrary to an inference some draw from the verse.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الركوب أعظم منافعها اقتصر عليه، ولا يدل ذلك على أنه لا يجوز لكل الخيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The different constructions of riding and adornment reflect their agents: the created beings ride, while the Creator makes the animals adornment, so the first takes li and the second direct accusative.
rows.anchor: لأن التقدير: خلقها، والركوب من صفات المخلوق لهم ذلك فانتفى شرط النصب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah parses zinatan as an accusative with an omitted verb, “and We made them adornment.”
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وزينة نصب بإضمار فعل تقديره: وجعلناها زينة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās a reading without the conjunction: “for you to ride them as adornment.”
rows.anchor: وروى قتادة عن ابن عباس: لتركبوها زينة بغير واو

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawāmiʿ treats zinah as a verbal noun used as a noun and parses it as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in “created them” or “ride them.”
rows.anchor: والزينة مصدر أقيم مقام الاسم، وانتصابه على الحال من الضمير في خلقها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads the phrase as God creating the animals as adornment for riding, or as adornment attached circumstantially to the pronoun in “ride them.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أي وخلقها زينة لتركبوها، أو يجعل زينة حالا من هاء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says that in the latter parsing zinah is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in “you ride them.”
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: والنصب حينئذ على الحال من الهاء في تركبوها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most interpreters take “what you do not know” broadly as humans, animals, and inanimate creations made for people’s benefit; their unknown variety adds evidence of God’s power, while their full knowledge is wisely withheld and beyond human grasp.
rows.anchor: فقال الجمهور: المعنى ما لا تعلمون من الآدميين والحيوانات والجمادات التي خلقها كلها لمنافعكم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah says the phrase refers to creatures whose origins are unknown, such as pests in plants and worms in fruit.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ما لا تعلمون، أصل حدوثه كالسوس في النبات والدود في الفواكه

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn Baḥr says the phrase means that people do not know how God creates those things.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن بحر: لا تعلمون كيف يخلقه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil identifies them as the unseen delights God prepared for His friends in Paradise, never seen or heard and beyond human thought.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: هو ما أعد الله لأوليائه في الجنة ما لا عين رأت

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī adds that the phrase includes what God prepared in Paradise and in the Fire for their inhabitants.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: وزاد بعد في الجنة وفي النار لأهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Various explanations are also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Shaʿbī, but the author leaves their reliability to God.
rows.anchor: ورويت تفاسير في: ما لا تعلمون في الحديث عن ابن عباس، ووهب بن منبه، والشعبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The broad reference to unknown creations follows the detailed account of useful animals, since the remaining animals’ uses are not usually beneficial and their details are countless.
rows.anchor: ويقال: لما ذكر الحيوان الذي ينتفع به انتفاعا ضروريا وغير ضروري، أعقب بذكر الحيوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaṣd is the verbal noun of intending a destination without turning away; al-sabīl is formally singular and may be singular in meaning, with the definite article referring to the revealed law’s path rather than a generic class.
rows.anchor: والقصد مصدر يقصد الوجه الذي يؤمه السالك لا يعدل عنه، والسبيل هنا مفرد اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading God clarifies the path of guidance by establishing proofs and sending messengers.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: وعلى الله تبيين طريق الهدى، وذلك بنصب الأدلة وبعثة الرسل

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah offers another reading: whoever follows the straight path has God’s mercy and bliss as his destination.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: ويحتمل أن يكون المعنى: إن من سلك الطريق القاصد فعلى الله رحمته ونعيمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “the path” is the covenant path of divine law, “from it” can refer back to that implicitly mentioned path because the deviant way is its understood opposite.
rows.anchor: لأن مقابلها يدل عليها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah also takes “from it” as a partitive reference to the law’s path, meaning deviant sects and branches within the community of Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يعود منها على سبيل الشرع، وتكون من للتبعيض، والمراد: فرق الضلالة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes al-sabīl generically: it divides into the path of truth and the deviant path of falsehood; jāʾir is what departs from upright guidance, as the cited poems illustrate.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ال في السبيل للجنس، وانقسمت إلى مصدر وهو طريق الحق، وإلى جائر وهو طريق الباطل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says God is bound to guide people along the path to truth, citing “Upon Us is guidance.”
rows.anchor: ومعنى قوله: وعلى الله قصد السبيل أن هداية الطريق الموصل إلى الحق واجبة عليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that the shift to “from it is a deviation” distinguishes the path attributable to God from the other; otherwise the verse would attribute both paths to Him, as determinists supposedly claim.
rows.anchor: ليعلم بما يجوز إضافته إليه من السبيلين وما لا يجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān characterizes al-Zamakhsharī’s argument as a Muʿtazilite interpretation.
rows.anchor: وهو تفسير على طريقة الاعتزال

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd’s reading says “among you is one who deviates,” namely one who chooses deviation; God disavows him.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله: ومنكم جائر يعني ومنكم جائر عن القصد بسواء اختياره

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī understands “had guided you all” as guidance by compulsion and coercion.
rows.anchor: ولو شاء لهداكم أجمعين قسرا والجاء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes “from them” refer to creatures: some creatures turn away from the truth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الضمير في ومنها يعود على الخلائق أي: ومن الخلائق جائر عن الحق

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: The reading attributed to ʿĪsā, “among you is one who deviates,” supports taking the pronoun as referring to creatures; it also appears in Ibn Masʿūd’s codex, while ʿAlī reads with faʾ.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده قراءة عيسى: ومنكم جائر، وكذا هي في مصحف عبد الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the deviants as adherents of different religions; another view specifies Jews, Christians, and Magians.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هم أهل الملل المختلفة. وقيل: اليهود والنصارى والمجوس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation says God would create guidance in you so none would go astray; the phrase is described as a will of choice.
rows.anchor: ولهداكم: لخلق فيكم الهداية، فلم يضل أحد منكم، وهي مشيئة الاختيار

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says God could have imposed a sign that compelled people to guidance and faith.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: لفرض عليكم آية تضطركم إلى الاهتداء والإيمان

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls al-Zajjāj’s view a bad position of innovators who deny that God creates human acts, and claims al-Zajjāj adopted it unwittingly.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا قول سوء لأهل البدع الذين يرون إن الله لا يخلق أفعال العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān corrects Ibn ʿAṭiyyah: al-Zajjāj was a Muʿtazilite, so the claim that he made this point accidentally is mistaken.
rows.anchor: ولم يعرف ابن عطية أن الزجاج معتزلي، فلذلك تأول أنه لم يحصله

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the phrase could mean guiding people to reward or Paradise without their deserving it.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: لو شاء لهداكم إلى الثواب، أو إلى الجنة بغير استحقاق

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God could have willed to make only the straight path, without the deviant one.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: لو شاء لمحض قصد السبيل دون الجائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object of “willed” is understood from “He would have guided you”: “had He willed your guidance.”
rows.anchor: ومفعول شاء محذوف لدلالة لهداكم أي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning creation and livestock, the passage recalls water as the basis of human and animal life and their provisions, then night, day, sun, moon, and earthly creations as favors.
rows.anchor: أنه لما امتن بإيجادهم بعد العدم وإيجاد ما ينتفعون به من الأنعام وغيرها من الركوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “for you” may modify water as an omitted adjective, govern the following “drink,” attach to “sent down,” or begin a fresh clause with “drink” as subject.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن لكم، في موضع الصفة لماء، فيتعلق بمحذوف، ويرتفع شراب به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning water’s descent, the verse divides its uses; “drink” means what is drunk and “from it” is straightforwardly partitive.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر إنزال الماء أخذ في تقسيمه. والشراب هو المشروب، والتبعيض في منه ظاهر، وأما في منه شجر فمجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From it grows vegetation” is figurative: trees are attributed to water because they grow through irrigation, like speaking of camels’ humps as being in rainclouds.
rows.anchor: وأما في منه شجر فمجاز، لما كان الشجر إنباته على سقيه بالماء جعل الشجر من الماء

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī explains the phrase through an omitted noun: either “from its source/irrigation grow trees,” or “trees drink,” as in the verse about love of the calf entering hearts.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: هو على حذف المضاف، إما قبل الضمير أي: ومن جهته

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says shajar means all that the earth grows, including pasture grass, as shown by a cited line about feeding meat when pasture is scarce.
rows.anchor: والشجر هنا كل ما تنبته الأرض قاله الزجاج. وقال: نطعمها اللحم إذا عز الشجر

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutaybah takes shajar here to mean pasture grass.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: الشجر هنا الكلأ

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: A report from ʿIkrimah quotes the prohibition “do not eat shajar,” explaining shajar as pasture grass and calling it unlawful gain.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث عكرمة: «لا تأكلوا الشجر فإنه سحت» يعني الكلأ

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives grazing livestock terminology from simah, a mark, because animals leave traces on the ground.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: من السومة، وهي العلامة، لأنها تؤثر في الأرض علامات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asāma and sawwama mean to send livestock out to graze; sāmat means it grazed freely, and sāʾimah/suwām describes grazing animals.
rows.anchor: ويقال: أسام الماشية وسومها جعلها ترعى، وسامت بنفسها فهي سائمة وسوام

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads tasīmūna with an open tāʾ; if the verb is transitive it equals asāma, while an intransitive reading implies “your livestock graze.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: تسيمون بفتح التاء، فإن سمع متعديا كان هو وأسام بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If shajar means all vegetation, the following crops continue the list; if it means pasture, the verse separately states another benefit of water.
rows.anchor: أخذ في ذكر غالب ما ينتفع به من الشجر إن كان المراد من قوله: ومنه شجر العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ’s cited line uses anbat for “grew,” supplying evidence for an intransitive use.
rows.anchor: رأيت ذوي الحاجات حول بيوتهم ... قطينا بهم حتى إذا أنبت البقل

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī rejects using anbat intransitively with the meaning “grew.”
rows.anchor: وكان الأصمعي يأبى أنبت بمعنى نبت

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr reads with the first-person plural nūn, “We grow.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر: ننبت بنون العظمة

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads the verb with gemination; an alternative view says this marks repetition or abundance.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري: ننبت بالتشديد قيل: للتكثير والتكرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān’s preferred explanation of the gemination is intensified causation.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أنه تضعيف التعدية

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads yanbut from intransitive nabata and puts “crops” and its coordinated nouns in the nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: ينبت من نبت ورفع الزرع وما عطف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four crops are singled out as the noblest and most useful: grain as the world’s main food, olives for lighting, eating, seasoning and ointment, dates as fine fruit and staple in some lands, and grapes as fruit alone.
rows.anchor: وخص الأربعة بالذكر لأنها أشرف ما ينبت، وأجمعه للمنافع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Some of every fruit” is partitive because the earth contains only some of all fruits, while all kinds will be in Paradise; this wording prompts reflection.
rows.anchor: لأن كل الثمرات لا تكون إلا في الجنة، وإنما أنبت في الأرض بعض من كلها للتذكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general phrase about fruits follows the pattern of mentioning unknown creatures: detailed varieties, forms, qualities, and uses cannot be counted.
rows.anchor: تنبيها على أن تفصيل القول في أجناسها وأنواعها وصفاتها ومنافعها مما لا يكاد يحصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing sign invites contemplation because a seed absorbs moisture, splits, sends a shoot upward and roots downward, then develops diverse leaves, flowers, fruit, and benefits through God’s deliberate power.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى أن الحبة الواحدة إذا وضعت في الأرض ومر عليها مقدار من الزمان معين لحقها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers put the sun and following nouns in the accusative, with musakhkharāt as an emphatic circumstantial accusative if read as a passive participle.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: والشمس وما بعده منصوبا، وانتصب مسخرات على أنها حال مؤكدة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī alternatively treats musakhkharāt as a plural verbal noun: God subjected the celestial bodies by various acts of subjugation.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون المعنى: أنه سخرها أنواعا من التسخير جمع مسخر

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads the sun and following nouns in the nominative as a new subject with a predicate; Ḥafṣ makes “the stars are subjugated” nominative too, readings that weaken al-Zamakhsharī’s verbal-noun parsing.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر: والشمس وما بعده بالرفع على الابتداء والخبر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and others read “the winds are subjugated” in place of “the stars,” a reading that differs from the codex consonantal text.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود، والأعمش، وابن مصرف: والرياح مسخرات في موضع

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash parses “the stars” as accusative under an omitted “He made”; then musakhkharāt is either the second object of jaʿala meaning “made,” or an explanatory circumstantial phrase if it means “created.”
rows.anchor: الأخفش: والنجوم منصوب على إضمار فعل تقديره: وجعل النجوم مسخرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subjugation of the celestial lights was explained earlier in the commentary on al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: وتقدم شرح تسخير هذه النيرات في الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse uses plural “signs” and reason because the celestial proofs are numerous and especially clear witnesses to divine power and majesty; the previous plant proof was one process despite its many varieties.
rows.anchor: لأن الآثار العلوية أظهر دلالة على القدرة الباهرة، وأبين شهادة للكبرياء والعظمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What He spread through the earth” is coordinated with night and day and includes animals, plants, fruits, and other creations of different colors.
rows.anchor: وما درأ معطوف على الليل والنهار يعني: ما خلق فيها من حيوان وشجر وثمر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the variation in color to mean different kinds, as in speaking of kinds of fruit or food; a further view means minerals.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مختلفا ألوانه أصنافه كما تقول: هذه ألوان من الثمر ومن الطعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In that is a sign” can refer to the created variety in this condition or specifically to the differences in color.
rows.anchor: إن في ذلك أي: فيما ذرأ على هذه الحال من اختلاف الألوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing “they remember” means taking heed of what had been forgotten: the subjection of created things on earth.
rows.anchor: وختم هذا بقوله: يذكرون، ومعناه الاعتبار والاتعاظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After discussing earthly creations, the passage turns to the sea’s subjection as a favor; its users can travel, dive for its contents, and fish.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى الاستدلال بما ذرأ في الأرض، ذكر ما امتن به من تسخير البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-baḥr is generic and includes salt and fresh water; its subjection enables travel, diving, and fishing.
rows.anchor: ومعنى تسخيره: كونه يتمكن الناس من الانتفاع به للركوب في المصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names food first as the most important use; “from it” elliptically means from its animals, and then mentions pearl and coral adornment, especially wearing it.
rows.anchor: وبدأ أولا من منافعه بما هو الأهم وهو الأكل، ومنه على حذف مضاف أي: لتأكلوا من حيوانه طريا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Fresh water is said rarely to yield pearls, which are mainly used medicinally; the source also mentions a sea-born emerald.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن العذب يخرج منه لؤلؤ لا يلبس إلا قليلا وإنما يتداوى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eating the fish applies to men and women, but wearing jewelry is specifically about women; it is attributed to men because women adorn themselves for them and so count as their adornment.
rows.anchor: فأما لتأكلوا فعام في النساء والرجال، وأما تلبسونها فخاص بالنساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ships are described as cleaving through the water, or as making a sound while parting it, carrying provisions and goods for trade.
rows.anchor: ذكر نعمة تصرف الفلك فيه ماخرة أي: شاقة فيه، أو ذات صوت لشق الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular address “you see” interrupts the plural address between the two purpose clauses; the following purpose may attach directly to the prior one or to an omitted purpose or verb.
rows.anchor: وأسند الرؤية إلى المخاطب المفرد فقال: وترى، وجعلها جملة معترضة بين التعليلين

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī allows “so that you may seek His bounty” to coordinate with an unexpressed cause or an omitted verb meaning “He did this so that you may seek.”
rows.anchor: وأجاز ابن الأنباري أن يكون معطوفا على علة محذوفة أي: لتبتغوا بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s bounty here means commercial profits and reaching distant lands; the verse indicates that sea travel is permissible.
rows.anchor: والفضل هنا حصول الأرباح بالتجارة، والوصول إلى البلاد الشاسعة، وفي هذا دليل على جواز ركوب البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to gratitude is for the blessings God has granted.
rows.anchor: ولعلكم تشكرون، على ما منحكم من هذه النعم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report says the earth initially convulsed after its creation and angels feared it would not support anyone; by morning mountains anchored it, though the angels did not know what they were made from. It is also transmitted from Wahb ibn Munabbih.
rows.anchor: قيل: خلق الله الأرض فجعلت تمور فقالت الملائكة: ما هي بمقر أحد على ظهرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rivers” is coordinated with “mountains”; alqā means “made,” supported by other Qurʾānic descriptions of making mountains and earth.
rows.anchor: وعطف وأنهارا على رواسي. ومعنى ألقى: جعل، ألا ترى إلى قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah argues that alqā is more specific than “created” or “made”: God brought mountains into being by His power and invention, rather than from the earth itself.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: قال المتأولون: ألقى بمعنى خلق وجعل، وهي عندي أخص من خلق وجعل

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah supports his interpretation with the story of the unstable earth and says it is also narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد هذا النظر ما روي في القصص عن الحسن، عن قيس بن عباد

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah parses “and rivers” with an implied verb, “He made” or “created”; he argues that the shared ellipsis proves alqā is more specific than “created.”
rows.anchor: وقوله: وأنهارا، منصوب بفعل مضمر تقديره: وجعل، أو خلق أنهارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyyah’s claim of consensus: interpreters explicitly report that alqā means “created” or “made.”
rows.anchor: وأي إجماع في هذا، وقد حكي عن المتأولين أن ألقى بمعنى خلق وجعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī supplies an implied “He made rivers,” since alqā carries the sense of jaʿala, and cites the earth-as-bed verse.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وأنهارا، وجعل فيها أنهارا لأن ألقى فيه معنى جعل

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ says the phrase may mean that God split rivers, and that “landmarks” means placing signs; the latter may coordinate with mountains.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: أي وشق أنهارا وعلامات أي: وضع علامات

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī notes that rational sciences establish that most rivers begin at mountain springs, explaining why rivers follow mountains in the sequence.
rows.anchor: ثبت في العلوم العقلية أن أكثر الأنهار إنما تتفجر منابعها في الجبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The roads lead to people’s destinations and allow them to find their way; another interpretation makes the guidance a lesson toward the Creator, truth, and God’s religion.
rows.anchor: وسبلا طرقا إلى مقاصدكم لعلكم تهتدون بالسبل إلى مقاصدكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī defines landmarks as features travelers use for orientation, such as mountains and plains; Abū Ḥayyān says this is also Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation.
rows.anchor: وعلامات هي معالم الطرق، وكل ما يستدل به السابلة من جبل وسهل

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says he saw groups identify roads by smelling the soil.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: ورأيت جماعة يتعرفون الطرقات بشم التراب

rows.speaker: ابن عيسى
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĪsā defines a sign as a form that communicates an intended meaning through writing, speech, gesture, or appearance.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عيسى: العلامة صورة يعلم بها ما يراد من خط أو لفظ أو إشارة أو هيئة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah treats “landmarks” as a verbal-noun-like accusative: these things serve as lessons and indications along every route, and mountains, rivers, and roads can all guide.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وعلامات نصب كالمصدر أي: فعل هذه الأشياء لعلكم تعتبرون بها

rows.speaker: ابن الكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Kalbī identifies the landmarks as mountains.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الكلبي: العلامات الجبال

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī and Mujāhid identify the landmarks as stars.
rows.anchor: وقال النخعي ومجاهد: النجوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unusual explanation calls the landmarks long, thin, snake-like fish in the Indian Ocean; their appearance signals arrival in India and safety on the route from Yemen.
rows.anchor: وأغرب ما فسرت به العلامات أنها حيتان طوال رقاق كالحيات في ألوانها وحركاتها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers have al-najm as a generic collective noun; Ibn Waththāb and al-Ḥasan read it with dammah, and authorities transmit these forms from ʿĀṣim’s circle.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وبالنجم، على أنه اسم جنس، ويؤيد ذلك قراءة ابن وثاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vocalized form is best taken as a collective plural, like saqf/saquf and rahn/ruhun, rather than as “stars” with a deleted wāw.
rows.anchor: وجعله مما جمع على فعل أولى من حمله على أنه أراد النجوم، فحذف الواو

rows.speaker: ابن عصفور
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṣfūr says using the singular al-najm for stars is forced by poetic necessity and cites a verse about the star’s disappearance.
rows.anchor: إلا أن ابن عصفور ذكر أن قولهم: النجم من ضرورة الشعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second poem uses “throats” in the singular-like hilaqīm form to mean plural throats, offered as a parallel.
rows.anchor: مثل قوله: حتى إذا ابتلت حلاقيم الحلق يريد: الحلوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sukūn in the reading is explained either as a lightened pronunciation or as a dialect form.
rows.anchor: والتسكين: قيل تخفيف، وقيل: لغة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identifies the star with the Pleiades, the two Firqads, Banāt Naʿsh, and al-Jady; al-Farrāʾ identifies it as al-Jady and the two Firqads.
rows.anchor: وعن السدي: هو الثريا، والفرقدان، وبنات نعش، والجدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jady here is the seventh of the smaller Banāt Naʿsh, while the two Firqads are its first two stars; this is distinct from al-Jady as a lunar station.
rows.anchor: قيل: والجدي هو السابع من بنات نعش الصغرى، والفرقدان الأولان منها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports asking the Prophet about “by the star,” and the Prophet identified it as al-Jady.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث عن ابن عباس أنه سأل الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم عن قوله: وبالنجم، فقل: «هو الجدي»
